transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
U.S. stock markets plunged yesterday, turning in their worst performance since April 2025.
The Dow lost more than 1,800 points yesterday as investors worried about the future of the
AI industry.
This morning, Dow futures are down more than 500 points in pre-market trading.
The Labor Department offers an update on the job market in about half an hour.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports forecasters expected to show a modest pickup in hiring last month.
Economists estimate that U.S. employers added around 60,000 jobs in October.
That would be about double the number of jobs added in September and slightly above the
average pace of hiring for the last three months.
New applications for unemployment benefits have remained consistently low, suggesting
that not many workers are being laid off in the current environment.
People who do lose a job, however, are taking longer, on average, to find new work.
The lack of turnover in the job market has kept a lid on pay raises.
Average wages have risen only about 3 percent in the last year.
That's not enough to keep pace with rising prices, which is a major concern for voters
in this week's midterm elections.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
An outgoing Republican member of the House has indicated he'll press on with efforts
to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Kentucky Republican Congressman Thomas Massie has already introduced the articles and says
he'll pursue them when the House reconvenes for its lame duck session.
Hegseth has released a video vowing to fight this.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries says his caucus will also examine the impeachment
articles.
We'll have that conversation when we gather as a caucus immediately upon our return.
But I've been very clear about my position with respect to Pete Hegseth.
He's the most unqualified secretary of defense in American history.
He should never have been confirmed.
He spoke to NPR's Morning Edition.
Prediction market Kalshi says it is referring at least half a dozen midterm election bettors
to federal law enforcement.
Kalshi and its rival Polly Market have faced pressure from lawmakers who are concerned
with insider trading and market manipulation.
NPR's Luke Garrett.
Kalshi says it has identified nearly 200 political candidates and over 14,000 campaign
staffers on its financial marketplace.
The prediction market was responding to a letter from Senators Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts
Democrat, and John Curtis, a Utah Republican.
Warren and Curtis requested information from Kalshi and its rival Polly Market on their
surveillance of insider trading and market manipulation ahead of the midterms.
In May, NPR reported that a campaign staffer made thousands betting on their own candidate
using insider information on prediction markets.
Kalshi now says it has launched around 60 investigations into potentially nefarious
election bets.
More than a dozen remain active, and at least six of these midterm bets are being referred
to law enforcement.
NPR's Luke Garrett reporting.
This is NPR.
European authorities say there has been a spate of new bomb threats today against passenger
flights.
Several have been called into planes flying to and from Czechia, media organizations in
Ireland say they've gotten threats, too.
Irish authorities say the threats to the media come on the heels of the threats of violence
against the European flights, and they appear to be a coordinated campaign of disruption.
Watching aggression can rewire the brain to be ready to fight.
That's the finding in a new study of mice, and NPR's Ping Huang reports on the study
that involved staged cage matches.
Mice that watched a series of staged cage fights, but had never fought themselves, showed
changes in their brains similar to those with actual fighting experience.
Anagrit Faulkner is with the Princeton Neuroscience Institute.
Watching doesn't get you the whole way there, but it does quite a fair bit, and it does
it all in the right direction.
Later, when the spectator mice had their own fights, they were more vigilant and used aggression
and defense strategies they picked up from watching both sides of a battle.
Their brain activity showed they had less inhibition, fewer neurons saying stop.
Faulkner says this demonstrates how just watching something can lead to changes in brain wiring
and behavior.
The paper is published in the journal Nature, Ping Huang, NPR News.
The weather is cleared on the border between southern Tennessee and northern Georgia.
Heavy flooding forced people to evacuate yesterday and submerged homes and businesses.
The National Weather Service says the rain over Blue Ridge, Georgia was a one in a thousand
year event.
More than ten inches of rain fell in about six hours.
This is NPR.

topics.text: U.S. stock markets plunge, Dow loses over 1,800 points on AI industry worries
Labor Department jobs report expected to show modest October hiring pickup, around 60,000 jobs
Rep. Thomas Massie plans to pursue impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in lame duck session
Kalshi refers at least six midterm election bettors to federal law enforcement over insider trading
European authorities report new bomb threats against passenger flights to and from Czechia
Study finds watching cage fights rewires mouse brains toward aggression, published in Nature
Heavy flooding on Tennessee-Georgia border forces evacuations, Blue Ridge rain a one-in-a-thousand event
